title: DiffuMamba: High-Throughput Diffusion LMs with Mamba Backbone
one_liner: Diffusion language models run 8 times faster by swapping the slow Transformer backbone for a speedy Mamba backbone.
lead: Diffusion language models generate text step-by-step by gradually turning noise into words, unlike the normal way (one word at a time). But they have been slow because they use Transformers, which scan every pair of words in the text—a quadratic (squared-cost) job. This paper replaces that with Mamba, which processes each word only once and keeps a rolling summary in a fixed-size hidden state instead of comparing it to all others, reducing the cost from squared to linear. Since the summary is good enough for most tasks, it can match the quality while running 8 times faster on long texts.

problem.h2: Slow diffusion: Transformers scan every pair of words
paras: Diffusion language models build text by starting with noise and gradually cleaning it up over many steps, each step guessing which words should replace the noise. A naive person might think: use a Transformer to look at the whole sequence and make the guess. Transformers do this by computing a score for every pair of words to decide which ones are relevant to each other. But that score-computation is quadratic—if your text is 1000 words, you compute 1,000,000 pairs, then 1,000,000 pairs again at the next step. On very long texts this becomes impossibly slow.

To speed this up, engineers add a trick: save the computed scores from one step (called a key-value cache, or KV-cache) so they don't recompute them. But that cache grows with the text length, eating precious graphics-card memory. So Transformers are stuck: fast when answering with short texts, but slow and memory-hungry on long ones.

callout.html: DiffuMamba replaces the slow Transformer backbone with Mamba, which processes text in linear time (not squared time) and never needs a cache.

steps.b: Replace Transformer layers with Mamba layers
steps.text: Each Transformer block that scanned all pairs is swapped for a Mamba block that processes the sequence in one pass.
Both Transformer and Mamba read left-to-right and right-to-left so they see context from both directions.

steps.b: Optional hybrid: interleave Mamba and Transformer layers
steps.text: DiffuMamba-H alternates Mamba blocks (fast) with occasional Transformer blocks (precise), balancing speed and quality.
The backbone swaps but the diffusion objective stays: start with noise, predict which words replace it, step by step.

steps.b: Measure answer speed and memory on long texts
steps.text: Run the model on sequences of varying lengths and compare throughput (words per second) and memory used.

paras: The paper swaps out the sequence processor inside the diffusion model. Instead of a Transformer (which scores all pairs of words), it uses Mamba (which scans each word once in sequence). This single swap removes the quadratic cost and the cache problem.

hidden.name: Answer time per sequence length
paras: The hidden quantity is how the time to answer one denoising step grows as the text gets longer. For a Transformer, this cost grows quadratically (if the text is twice as long, answering takes four times longer). For Mamba, it grows linearly (twice as long text takes twice as long). The paper measures this by recording how many words per second the model generates on texts of different lengths.
Because Mamba processes each word only once (in a fixed-time hidden state) instead of comparing it to all other words, the total cost is proportional to the sequence length, not the length squared.

heat.caption: Darker means more time or memory. Mamba stays light even on long texts.

reads.html: The cost to process a text grows with its length. Transformers multiply the cost by the length squared; Mamba just multiplies by the length once. On a 100-word text both are fast, but on a 10,000-word text the Transformer takes 10,000 times longer while Mamba takes 100 times longer.

Transformer cost grows with the square of sequence length N; Mamba cost grows linearly with N via a recurrent state transition without explicit pairwise scoring, hence no KV-cache and flat throughput scaling.

mechanism.h2: Why Mamba is fast: recurrent scanning versus pairwise scoring
paras: A Transformer scores every word pair because it needs to know which words are related. It is like filing: to find which documents go together, you compare every pair (expensive). Mamba works differently. It reads the text left-to-right (and in a variant, right-to-left) and updates a single small hidden state as it goes, like a train moving along a track and picking up one piece of information at each station. The hidden state contains enough information to predict the next word; you do not need to score all pairs.

Because each word is processed exactly once—read in, update the state, predict, move on—the cost is linear in the text length. The trade-off is that Mamba has less direct context: it knows the past (via the hidden state) but the hidden state is a fixed size, so it can only hold a summary. Transformer can score word 1000 against word 2000 directly even if they are far apart. But in practice, for many tasks Mamba's summary is good enough, especially if the text is not pathologically long.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the hidden state is a list of 4 numbers: [2, 1, 3, 1]
A keeps 50% of the old state: multiply [2, 1, 3, 1] by 0.5 = [1, 0.5, 1.5, 0.5]
This state now carries information about all words seen so far, compact and updated once per word.

math.note: Instead of storing all word pairs in a cache, Mamba stores one small state and updates it one word at a time, making it linear-time.

items.b: Very long context forgets early details.
items.html: The hidden state is fixed-size, so on a very long text (50,000+ words), the state may not hold all the detail from early paragraphs. Transformer has no such problem because it can directly score word 1 against word 50,000. If the task requires remembering fine details from far apart, Mamba may lose them.

The matrices A and B control what the state remembers. These must be learned during training. If training is weak (too few examples or noisy data), Mamba may learn to save the wrong details. Transformers have the same problem but have been more widely studied, so engineers know more tricks to train them well.

If you add Transformer layers back to gain quality, you bring back the quadratic cost. The speedup shrinks. The paper shows a 4.3x speedup for DiffuMamba-H versus 8.2x for pure Mamba, because the interleaved Transformer layers still cost time.

items.b: Done right: measure both quality and speed.
items.html: On a standard benchmark (language modeling or text generation), confirm that Mamba diffusion matches Transformer diffusion in final text quality. Only then is the speedup a real win, not a loss disguised as efficiency.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small diffusion language model with both a Transformer backbone and a Mamba backbone, train both on the same dataset for the same number of steps, then measure: (1) final text quality (e.g., accuracy on a simple language task or a human-judged sentence score), (2) inference throughput in words per second on sequences of length 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and (3) peak graphics-card memory used. Plot inference time (y-axis) versus sequence length (x-axis) for both backbones. The Transformer curve should rise steeply (quadratic), while Mamba should stay nearly flat (linear).
demo.metric_eq: throughput = (total words generated) / (total inference time in seconds)
demo.closing: If Mamba stays fast and flat while Transformer gets slower on long sequences, and both achieve similar final text quality, the mechanism is proven: you swapped a bottleneck.
